title: arXiv AI daily — 28 October 2026: six notable papers on agent teams, data scaling, and grounded evaluation
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending or readership chart. This is an inferred, relevance-led selection; Semantic Scholar citation and influential-citation totals were zero for all selected papers at the snapshot, so recent-paper attention evidence is limited and the ordering is not a popularity ranking.

sections.title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
sections.abstract: TeamGym evaluates and trains language-model teams on decisions built from legal, finance, medical, and software corpora, and reports substantial communication and retrieval gaps when pivotal evidence is distributed among agents.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce pivotal information units and a configurable team benchmark, then report average success-rate drops of 22.9 percentage points from distributing pivotal evidence and another 19.9 points when teams must retrieve it from source material; two policy-training experiments improve final decisions and induce coordination.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors report one training run for each policy-training demonstration; on held-out MAUD problems, coordination patterns transfer more clearly than final-decision quality. Transfer to live teams and other task distributions is not established here.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The paper's 8-model, 12-corpus evaluation and controlled separation of communication from retrieval make it directly relevant to multi-agent capability measurement; an OpenReview listing provides a second checkable record. These are scope and discoverability signals, not readership statistics.

sections.title: Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis
sections.abstract: Across 458,752 synthetic tasks and 849 models of four sizes, the authors vary tool, task, and database diversity and report that scaling environment diversity and complexity can generalize better than simply adding tasks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce SynthAPI and an environment-composition scaling law; they report improved generalization when the synthetic-data budget favors broader tools and database states, and benchmark gains over prior synthesis approaches.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors state that SynthAPI has no user-in-the-loop interactions, underrepresents long-document retrieval, and validates its scaling law on only one data pipeline; they do not claim transfer to other pipelines or training settings.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: AITOP published a separate technical write-up of the SynthAPI findings, and the paper reports a large controlled study with four downstream evaluation benchmarks. Its scale and independent technical mention support placing it high for relevance; they do not establish popularity.

sections.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
sections.abstract: ThinkWorld represents actions as discrete Chains-of-Dynamics and uses predicted-versus-observed future states to train VLA action reasoning from both robot demonstrations and videos without action labels.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors propose a shared motion-token reasoning space and consequence-grounded reinforcement learning, using future-state agreement to extend action supervision to unlabeled human videos; they report human-to-robot transfer and generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors report training from a single seed, so their episode-level confidence intervals do not measure variation across independently trained checkpoints; inference latency also depends on the stated hardware and input setup.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: It is cross-listed across robotics, AI, and computer vision, and reports simulation plus real-robot evaluations; the authors also provide a project page. The breadth and concrete embodied-learning evidence make it a strong relevance pick, though not an external popularity signal.

sections.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
sections.abstract: On a controlled 480-task benchmark, rarity- and relevance-based memory filters fail under different distributions of supporting and decoy facts, while attribution tags can induce social-proof errors in the final decision model.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce CrossProfile, which crosses ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts while holding their text fixed; they report that neither rarest-first nor relevance-first selection is reliably better than random, and that removing or randomizing agent-attribution tags can improve accuracy in the classic hidden-profile setup.
sections.unique_caveat: The benchmark's controlled discussions and fixed four-agent setup isolate specific failure mechanisms; the authors note that group-size effects are not varied, and the natural-discussion experiment is narrower than the controlled benchmark.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The paper spans three core AI categories and isolates memory selection from evidence ownership using 60 templates and four model families; it is also listed in the Hugging Face Papers index. These are breadth and discoverability signals, not evidence of readership.

sections.title: RubricAtlas: Mining Type-Level Rubrics from Expert Reports to Evaluate Deep Research Agents
sections.abstract: RubricAtlas derives reusable analytical requirements from expert financial reports and evaluates deep-research reports through evidence-linked checkpoints, with completeness scored separately from argument validity.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors build type-level rubrics from multiple expert reports and report checkpoint agreement of κ=0.71 and agent-ranking agreement of Kendall τ=0.87 across two judge pipelines; controlled deletions lower scores on affected analyses.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors say their first-author audit is not independent expert validation, their source corpus is Chinese financial research, and generic argument-validity rules show limited judge agreement; completeness should not be read as correctness.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The study covers 3,079 reports, 99 research types, and ten agents; an independent SignalFieldNotes article discusses the work. Cross-category relevance and a checkable secondary discussion support its place among notable new papers, not a popularity claim.

sections.title: What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models
sections.abstract: Using six point-in-time model families and six benchmarks, the authors define a temporal variability score for item likelihoods and report that high-variability items improve faster later in pretraining, leading low-variability items in 34 of 36 final model-benchmark settings.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors define temporal variability score (TVS) from item-level negative log-likelihood variation across point-in-time models and report a 7.3-point average chance-normalized accuracy advantage for high-TVS items at the end of training, with the effect strongest on knowledge-intensive tasks.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors limit the evidence to likelihood-ranked multiple-choice benchmarks and a single-size PIT-4B model series covering web crawls from 2017–2024; contamination checks do not cover all evaluated models' pretraining corpora.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The arXiv record says the paper was accepted to AACL 2026, and its reported comparison spans six benchmarks and six models; it is included for direct relevance to training dynamics, not as a claim of unusual readership.
